content: The Joint Meeting on Pesticide Specifications (JMPS) is responsible for evaluating whether existing FAO/WHO specifications are applicable to certain pesticides. These specifications cover the physical appearance of the material, the content of active ingredients, relevant impurities, physical and chemical properties, and storage stability. However, they do not address the chemical characteristics of formulants unless these affect physical properties such as pH, acidity, or alkalinity. Additionally, the specifications do not define the fundamental properties or efficacy of the active ingredient, as the JMPS does not evaluate pesticide efficacy. FAO specifications for agricultural pesticides are developed only after the manufacturer has registered the product in one or more countries, with efficacy inferred from this evidence. For public health pesticides, the efficacy of active ingredients and formulations is evaluated through laboratory and field trials by the WHO Pesticide Evaluation Scheme (WHOPES), typically during the development of WHO/FAO specifications for the technical material. WHO specifications for formulations are published after satisfactory safety and efficacy evaluations. In special cases, interim specifications or guidelines may be introduced for novel public health products under evaluation. Hazard and risk evaluations for these specifications are primarily based on assessments by national registration authorities or other international organizations. If such evaluations are unavailable, FAO/WHO arranges a detailed assessment of original studies before the JMPS develops specifications. A critical aspect of hazard and risk assessment is determining the relationship between the submitted purity/impurity profile data and the limits applied during normal manufacturing. FAO and WHO recognize that generating duplicate data on all potential hazards for each pesticide manufacturer may be unnecessary and ethically undesirable. However, the absence of direct links between hazard data and manufacturing processes does not prevent the development or extension of specifications. The JMPS consists of scientists with expertise in developing pesticide specifications. Their recommendations to FAO/WHO are made in their individual expert capacities, not as representatives of their countries or organizations. The JMPS is a statutory body of FAO, with panel members appointed by the Director-General. WHO experts are drawn from its Panel of Experts on Vector Biology and Control. Representatives from other FAO or WHO units, as well as academic, government, or industry experts with specialized knowledge, may be invited to participate as advisors. The primary function of the JMPS is to provide recommendations to FAO and/or WHO on adopting, modifying, or withdrawing specifications. Wherever possible, test methods cited in FAO/WHO specifications should have been validated through inter-laboratory trials, such as those conducted by the Collaborative International Pesticides Analytical Council (CIPAC) or AOAC International. Methods for determining active ingredients or physical properties not validated by these organizations are accepted on a case-by-case basis. In disputes, designated referee methods, typically those from CIPAC or AOAC, are used unless proven inferior to another method. The Joint Meeting on Pesticide Residues (JMPR) evaluates acceptable daily intake (ADI), acute reference doses (ARfD), and maximum residue limits (MRLs) for pesticides. The JMPR proposed in 1999 that its evaluations of pesticide toxicology and residues should ideally follow the development of FAO/WHO specifications. This proposal was accepted by the Codex Committee on Pesticide Residues in 2001. However, harmonizing their agendas may take years, and alignment may not always be possible, especially for non-agricultural pesticides. FAO/WHO specifications are prioritized for review and potential withdrawal if the pesticide is subject to international conventions such as the Rotterdam Convention on Prior Informed Consent (PIC) or the Stockholm Convention on Persistent Organic Pollutants (POPs). Specifications may be retained if changes in formulation or impurity control reduce risks to acceptable levels. Specifications also align with international standards, such as ISO common names, INCI nomenclature for insect repellents, and OECD recommendations for pesticide registration. The development of FAO/WHO specifications relies on data provided by the pesticide industry. Manufacturers are encouraged to submit draft specifications and supporting data to the JMPS for evaluation. WHOPES assesses efficacy data provided by the industry to determine further testing requirements before developing formulation specifications. However, efficacy data are not considered by the JMPS. Manufacturers must inform FAO/WHO of any changes in manufacturing processes that could affect the validity of specifications, as well as changes in the manufacturer's name or contact information. Failure to provide this information may result in the withdrawal of the specification. Industry is also encouraged to prepare draft guideline specifications for new formulation types for JMPS consideration. These guidelines are reviewed and updated as needed. FAO/WHO specifications are intended to enhance confidence in pesticide quality, contributing to human and environmental safety, sustainable agriculture, and improved public health. They may serve as international reference points for national authorities but do not replace national or international registration requirements. The JMPS holds annual open and closed meetings to evaluate and confirm new or revised specifications, resolve disputes, and update its agenda. Open meetings allow discussion of general issues, while closed meetings address commercially confidential information. Additional experts may be invited to provide input on contentious issues but are required to maintain confidentiality and are not involved in final recommendations. FAO and WHO maintain the confidentiality of all information provided in support of proposed specifications.
